paragraphs.heading: Matter we cannot see
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is an invisible and hypothetical kind of matter that does not interact with electromagnetic radiation, light included. We infer it from gravitational effects that general relativity cannot explain unless there is more matter than we observe. These effects turn up in how galaxies form and change, in gravitational lensing, in how galaxies move inside galaxy clusters, and in the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background.

paragraphs.heading: How much there is
paragraphs.text: In the standard Lambda-CDM model of cosmology, 68.2% of the universe's mass–energy is dark energy, which is a form of energy, while 26.8% is dark matter and 5% is ordinary matter. So dark matter makes up 85% of all mass, and dark matter and dark energy together make up 95% of the total. Dark matter is dense in the halo around a galaxy, yet in the Solar System it is much sparser than normal matter. All of it out to Neptune's orbit adds up to about 10¹⁷ kg, roughly the mass of a large asteroid.

paragraphs.heading: The scaffolding of the cosmos
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is thought to act as gravitational scaffolding for cosmic structures. After the Big Bang it gathered into blobs along narrow filaments, while superclusters of galaxies formed a cosmic web on scales where whole galaxies look like tiny particles. Physicists sort dark matter into cold, warm or hot by its speed, or more exactly its free streaming length. Recent models lean toward cold dark matter, in which structures appear as particles gradually build up.

paragraphs.heading: What could it be
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is not known to interact with ordinary matter or radiation except through gravity, which makes it hard to detect in a lab. The most popular explanation is an undiscovered subatomic particle, such as weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) or axions. The other main option is primordial black holes. A minority of astrophysicists argue instead for changing the laws of gravity, with ideas such as modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND), yet none of these theories fits all the evidence at once.

paragraphs.heading: Zwicky and the Coma Cluster
paragraphs.text: In 1933 Swiss astrophysicist Fritz Zwicky, working at Caltech, studied the Coma Cluster of galaxies. He weighed it using the motions of galaxies near its edge, compared that with an estimate from its brightness and galaxy count, and found about 400 times more mass than could be seen. He named the unseen mass dunkle Materie, or dark matter, and argued that its gravity held the cluster together. His figures were off by more than an order of magnitude, mostly because of an outdated value of the Hubble constant, but he was right that most of the gravitating matter was dark. Unlike modern theories, though, he pictured it as ordinary matter that does not shine.

paragraphs.heading: Older hints
paragraphs.text: The idea had earlier roots. In 1906 Henri Poincaré used the French phrase matière obscure, meaning dark matter, though he decided there was less of it than visible matter, which later proved false. Jacobus Kapteyn argued for it from the speeds of stars in 1922, and a 1930 paper by Knut Lundmark suggests he was the first to propose that the universe holds much more mass than we can see. Jan Oort also proposed it in 1932, but his measurement was later found to be wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Clues from spinning galaxies
paragraphs.text: The dark matter hypothesis largely took hold in the 1970s, when several lines of evidence were brought together to argue that galaxies are wrapped in halos of unseen matter. In 1974 two independent groups, one in Princeton, New Jersey, and one in Tartu, Estonia, reached this conclusion. A key clue was the shape of galaxy rotation curves. Vera Rubin and Kent Ford used a new spectrograph to measure these curves for edge-on spiral galaxies, while radio astronomers mapped how atomic hydrogen in nearby galaxies shines in the 21 cm line.
